case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Home cooks and culinary enthusiasts will adopt a consumer vacuum sealer if they perceive it as a professional-grade tool that improves food freshness and reduces waste, leading to multiple purchases per household. Who benefits: Consumers seeking to preserve food quality and save money; MULTIVAC benefits by capturing premium pricing and repeat purchases.. Why behaviour changes: Growing interest in sous vide cooking and bulk food processing creates a demand for reliable, airtight sealing; current chamber sealers are already used by professional chefs and home enthusiasts, signaling quality.. How value is captured: MULTIVAC can price the consumer model at a premium (e.g., €200-€300) and sell accessories (bags, seals) and service contracts, generating recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Home users have sufficient disposable income to justify the price.; Marketing can effectively communicate professional-grade performance.; Distribution channels (online, specialty retailers) can reach target consumers.. Predictions: Surveyed home cooks will indicate willingness to pay ≥€200 for a vacuum sealer.; Purchase intent will be higher when described as a professional-grade tool.; Repeat purchase rate for accessories will be ≥20% within 12 months..

T2: Health‑conscious consumers will adopt a consumer vacuum sealer if they perceive it as a way to preserve nutrients and reduce food waste, leading to purchase decisions based on environmental and health benefits. Who benefits: Consumers concerned about nutrition retention and waste reduction; MULTIVAC benefits by positioning the product as a sustainable, health‑focused offering and can command premium pricing.. Why behaviour changes: Growing awareness of food waste and nutrient loss drives demand for packaging that maintains freshness and quality; current evidence shows consumers already value vacuum sealing for freshness.. How value is captured: MULTIVAC can market the consumer model as a health‑preserving tool, price it at a premium (e.g., €200‑€300), and sell accessories and subscription services for reusable bags, capturing recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for products that reduce waste.; Marketing can effectively communicate nutrient retention benefits.; Distribution can reach health‑focused consumers (specialty retailers, online health platforms).. Predictions: Surveyed health‑conscious consumers will indicate willingness to pay ≥€200 for a vacuum sealer marketed on nutrient retention.; Purchase intent will be higher when highlighted as a waste‑reducing solution.; Repeat purchase rate for accessories will be ≥20% within 12 months when positioned as health‑focused..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Professional-Grade vs. Health-Focused Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with between‑subjects design.. Sample: 200 German adults aged 25–55, self‑identified home cooks or food enthusiasts, recruited via panel providers.. Measure: 1) Willingness to pay (WTP) for a vacuum sealer priced at €250 (premium). 2) Purchase intent under professional‑grade framing (description of chamber sealers as professional‑grade tools for sous vide). 3) Purchase intent under health‑focused framing (description of chamber sealers as preserving nutrients and reducing waste).. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP and purchase intent under professional‑grade framing than under health‑focused framing.; T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent under health‑focused framing than under professional‑grade framing.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the professional‑grade framing is at least €15 higher than for the health‑focused framing (difference ≥ €15) and purchase intent for professional‑grade framing is at least 15 percentage points higher (difference ≥ 15%), then T1 is supported and the. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the vacuum sealer as a professional-grade tool for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing, priced at a premium (e.g., €250), and sold through specialty retailers and online channels. Begin with a limited launch to test demand before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-MULTIVAC-UPDATE concerns running costs and does not address professional-grade performance or health benefits. It does not affect T1's core premise that home cooks adopt a vacuum sealer because they perceive it as a professional-grade tool for sous vide and bulk food processing. New claim: Home cooks and culinary enthusiasts will adopt a consumer vacuum sealer if they perceive it as a professional-grade tool that improves food freshness and reduces waste, leading to multiple purchases per household.. Evidence: SYN-MULTIVAC-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the vacuum sealer as a professional-grade tool for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing, priced at a premium (e.g., €250), and sold through specialty retailers and online channels. Begin with a limited launch to test demand before scaling. Target customer: Home cooks and culinary enthusiasts who value professional-grade performance and are willing to pay a premium for reliable, airtight sealing for sous vide and bulk food processing.. Value proposition: A consumer vacuum sealer that delivers professional-grade sealing capabilities, reducing food waste and preserving freshness, while offering a premium, high‑margin product and recurring accessories sales.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed choice‑based conjoint survey (200 German home cooks, €15k, 10 weeks) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent under professional‑grade framing versus health‑focused framing.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, willingness to pay a premium, and the strength of repeat purchase behavior are uncertain. The survey will resolve these uncertainties.. Would change if: If the survey shows that health‑focused framing yields higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than professional‑grade framing, we would shift to a health‑focused positioning.; If the survey shows low overall willingness to pay or low purchase intent, we would reconsider expansion.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Direct-to-Consumer vs. Aftermarket Price Sensitivity Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are recruited from Italy, Germany, and the United States (markets with strong motorcycle/off-road culture). They are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a premium direct-to-consumer (DTC) offer for a Brembo brake kit (e.g., €750 for a motorcycle kit). Group B sees the same kit priced at €250 (aftermarket price). Both groups are asked: "Would you purchase this kit at the offered price?" (yes/no).. Sample: 300 participants (100 per group). Participants are screened for self-identified motorcycle/off-road enthusiasts (e.g., have ridden for >5 years, own a motorcycle/off-road vehicle).. Measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants who select "yes" to the DTC offer).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show a purchase intent rate of at least 30% (indicating willingness to pay premium for a branded DTC kit).; T2: Group B will show a purchase intent rate of at least 30% (indicating willingness to pay aftermarket price for a branded DTC kit).. Decision rule: If Group A’s purchase intent rate ≥ 30% and Group B’s ≤ 20%, proceed to develop a differentiated DTC proposition targeting enthusiasts. If both rates ≤ 20%, no expansion. If Group A ≥ 30% and Group B ≥ 30%,. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, conduct the proposed direct-to-consumer price sensitivity test (X1) to measure willingness to pay for a premium kit. If the test shows purchase intent above 30% for the €750 DTC offer, proceed to develop a differentiated DTC proposition targeting motorsport enthusiasts; otherwise, maintain the existing B2B and aftermarket focus. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Preference Survey for Biesse Consumer CNC" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view product description and pricing for a Biesse consumer CNC router. They indicate willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale and choose a preferred purchase channel (direct showroom, online marketplace, or retail store).. Sample: 500 DIY woodworkers (recruited via hobbyist forums) and 500 small‑batch manufacturers (recruited via makerspace networks and Etsy). Randomly split each group into two halves: half see a precision‑focused description, half see a speed‑of‑setup description.. Measure: Average WTP (EUR) for precision version vs speed version, and channel preference (showroom vs online vs retail). Secondary measure: self‑identified primary use case (personal projects vs small‑batch production).. Predictions: T1: DIY woodworkers will show higher WTP and higher showroom preference for the precision version, while small‑batch manufacturers will show higher WTP and higher online/retail preference for the speed version.; T2: Small‑batch manufacturers will show higher WTP and higher showroom/online preference for the speed version, while DIY woodworkers will show higher WTP and higher retail preference for the precision version.. Decision rule: If the average WTP difference between precision and speed versions exceeds €150 for the group that identifies as DIY woodworkers, proceed with a precision‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference exceeds €150 for the group that identifies as small‑batch. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Home Storage Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions. Sample: 400 Swiss consumers aged 25-55, recruited via panel, balanced for gender and region. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and maximum WTP (EUR) for two product concepts: (1) Standalone home storage unit priced at 20% premium over standard storage (e.g., €1,200 vs €1,000). (2) Subscription-based home storage kit with hardware, installation, maintenance, and consumables, priced at €1,500 per year.. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent for the standalone unit will be at least 15% and WTP will exceed €1,000; subscription intent will be low (e.g., <5%).; T2: Purchase intent for the subscription kit will be at least 10% and WTP will exceed €1,500; standalone intent will be low (e.g., <5%).. Decision rule: If standalone purchase intent ≥15% and subscription purchase intent <10%, proceed with a direct-to-consumer standalone launch. If subscription purchase intent ≥10% and standalone intent <5%, proceed with a subscription-based model. If both meet thresholds, consider a hybrid. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Home Storage Preference Test to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a standalone, premium-priced home storage unit. If the test meets the thresholds (purchase intent ≥15% and WTP >€1,000), proceed to develop a direct-to-consumer standalone offering; otherwise, consider a subscription model or no expansion. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE concerns a rental vs purchase choice for a compact automated storage module, not consumer demand for home storage. It does not address T1’s claim about standalone purchase intent or willingness to pay for a premium home unit. New claim: Consumers will adopt Kardex’s automated storage solutions for home use if they perceive a clear functional benefit (e.g., space savings, faster retrieval) and can afford the price, leading to repeat purchases.. Evidence: SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Run the proposed Home Storage Preference Test to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a standalone, premium-priced home storage unit. If the test meets the thresholds (purchase intent ≥15% and WTP >€1,000), proceed to develop a direct-to-consumer standalone offering; otherwise, consider a subscription model or no expansion. Target customer: Swiss consumers aged 25-55 who need efficient home storage and are willing to pay a premium for automated solutions.. Value proposition: A differentiated, premium-priced automated home storage unit that solves real storage problems, leveraging Kardex’s intelligent retrieval technology to deliver faster access and reduced clutter.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the 10‑week, €15,000 online conjoint survey with 400 participants to collect purchase intent and willingness‑to‑pay data for the standalone unit and a subscription kit.. Uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for automated home storage; the size of the addressable market; competitive response from established consumer storage brands; and the feasibility of direct‑to‑consumer distribution.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent below 10% or WTP below €1,000, the recommendation would shift toward a subscription model or no expansion.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for a subscription‑based model, the favoured theory could shift to T2.; If additional market research reveals a large, untapped segment of small‑business owners seeking automated storage, the focus could shift to B2B consumer‑focused offerings.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "DIY vs Contractor Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are recruited from a panel of DIY enthusiasts and professional contractors. They are shown a Sika-branded DIY sealant product description (easy-to-use, professional-grade results) and a Sika-branded contractor sealant product description (code-compliant, single supplier for both residential and commercial). They are then asked to indicate their likelihood to purchase each product on a 1‑10 scale. The. Sample: 200 participants: 100 DIY enthusiasts (recruited via DIY forums and social media) and 100 contractors (recruited via construction industry platforms).. Measure: Average purchase intent score for DIY product (T1) and contractor product (T2).. Predictions: T1: DIY participants will report a purchase intent score ≥ 7 for the DIY product and ≤ 5 for the contractor product.; T2: Contractors will report a purchase intent score ≥ 7 for the contractor product and ≤ 5 for the DIY product.. Decision rule: If the average DIY intent score ≥ 7 and contractor intent score ≤ 5, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting DIY (supports T1). If the average contractor intent score ≥ 7 and DIY intent score ≤ 5, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts for a specific use case (e.g., home waterproofing, flooring installation). Begin with a limited launch of a branded DIY sealant line, leveraging existing distribution channels (hardware stores, online marketplaces) and marketing that emphasizes ease-of-use and professional results. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer purchase behavior, ease of use, or professional-grade perception. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts for a specific use case (e.g., home waterproofing, flooring installation). Begin with a limited launch of a branded DIY sealant line, leveraging existing distribution channels (hardware stores, online marketplaces) and marketing that emphasizes ease-of-use and professional results. Target customer: Individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who need reliable sealants, adhesives, or waterproofing for home improvement projects.. Value proposition: A branded DIY sealant line that delivers professional-grade results while being easy to use, sold through trusted retail channels at a price comparable to leading store brands, capturing higher retail margins and brand extension.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed DIY vs Contractor Purchase Intent Test (200 participants, 10 weeks, €15,000) to validate purchase intent for the DIY product. If the test confirms DIY intent ≥7 and contractor intent ≤5, proceed to develop the consumer line. Uncertainty: The actual purchase behavior of homeowners and DIY buyers, the competitive response from existing consumer sealant brands, and the ability to communicate perceived ease of use and professional results effectively.. Would change if: If the test shows contractor intent ≥7 and DIY intent ≤5, indicating stronger contractor demand, the recommendation would shift to targeting contractors or a hybrid approach.; If new evidence shows that Sika already sells a significant volume of consumer products through retail channels, the case for expansion would weaken.; If a competitor launches a similar branded DIY sealant line before Sika, the competitive landscape would change.. T1: Homebrewers and small-batch food producers will adopt Krones equipment if they perceive it as a premium, reliable brand that reduces production time and cost, because they value quality and efficiency in their own products. Who benefits: Krones benefits by capturing higher-margin sales directly to consumers and by building brand loyalty that could extend to larger B2B contracts.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view Krones as a trusted, efficient solution, they will purchase equipment directly rather than relying on generic or competitor brands, shifting from B2B to direct-to-consumer sales.. How value is captured: Krones would sell branded, higher-priced machines directly to consumers, earning premium pricing and potentially subscription services or consumables.. Assumptions: Consumers in target segments (homebrewers, small-batch food makers) have sufficient discretionary income to afford Krones equipment.; Krones can communicate brand quality effectively to this segment.; Direct-to-consumer sales channels are feasible and cost-effective for Krones.. Predictions: A test offering a Krones homebrew machine at a premium price to a sample of 200 homebrewers will achieve at least 15% purchase intent compared to a generic competitor.; Surveyed consumers will rank Krones higher than competitors on reliability and ease of use..

T2: Homebrewers and small-batch food producers will adopt Krones equipment if they need a scalable, compliant solution for regulatory-compliant production, because they face stringent safety and labeling requirements that limit entry into larger markets. Who benefits: Krones benefits by selling integrated, compliant systems that lower customer risk and can be sold at premium prices, potentially locking in long-term contracts.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers recognize Krones as a provider of compliant, easy-to-use equipment, they will choose Krones to avoid costly retrofitting or legal issues, shifting from generic to branded solutions.. How value is captured: Krones would charge higher prices for compliant systems and offer service contracts to maintain regulatory validity, capturing recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Regulatory compliance is a significant barrier for small-batch producers entering larger markets.; Krones can demonstrate compliance and simplify the process for customers.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for compliance solutions.. Predictions: A test offering a Krones homebrew system with integrated compliance features to 150 small-batch producers will achieve at least 10% purchase intent compared to a generic competitor.; Surveyed producers will rank Krones higher than competitors on compliance support..

T1: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s precision tools if they perceive them as affordable, reliable, and compatible with existing CNC machines, because these attributes lower the perceived risk and cost of switching from other brands. Who benefits: Gühring benefits by capturing sales from a growing segment of individual buyers who value precision and compatibility, expanding its consumer market beyond B2B.. Why behaviour changes: If hobbyists view Gühring as a trusted, compatible alternative that performs as well as higher‑priced competitors, they will purchase it instead of cheaper alternatives or continue using existing tools.. How value is captured: Gühring can price its tools competitively while maintaining its premium reputation, generating revenue from a new consumer segment without diluting its industrial brand.. Assumptions: Hobbyists and small workshops have sufficient budget for precision tools.; They prioritize reliability and compatibility over cost.; They are aware of Gühring through existing B2B channels or word of mouth.. Predictions: If offered at a price 10‑20% below premium CNC tool brands, Gühring will achieve at least 5% market share among hobbyists within 12 months.; Customer surveys will show that compatibility with existing CNC machines is the top purchase driver for 60% of buyers..

T2: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s tools if they are marketed as a premium, status‑enhancing brand that signals expertise and craftsmanship, because status motivates purchase decisions beyond functional need. Who benefits: Gühring benefits by commanding premium prices and building a consumer brand that differentiates it from generic tools, potentially creating a new revenue stream and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: If hobbyists perceive Gühring as a brand that signifies high‑quality craftsmanship and expert‑level performance, they will choose it over cheaper alternatives even if the functional performance is similar.. How value is captured: Gühring can price its consumer line at a premium (e.g., 20‑30% above mainstream CNC tool brands) while leveraging its existing reputation for precision in industrial markets, capturing higher margins and brand equity.. Assumptions: Hobbyists value status and brand reputation in tools.; They are willing to pay more for a brand that signals expertise.; They are aware of Gühring through its industrial presence or word of mouth.. Predictions: If marketed as a premium brand, Gühring will achieve at least 3% market share among hobbyists within 12 months, even if functional performance is comparable to cheaper alternatives.; Surveyed buyers will rank “brand prestige” as the top purchase driver for 40% of purchases..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Low-Cost Proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with randomized exposure to either a premium-priced safety-focused proposition or a low-cost volume-focused proposition, followed by willingness-to-pay (WTP) and purchase intent questions.. Sample: 500 German consumers aged 25-55 who own or plan to purchase electric vehicles or home automation devices within 12 months, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and WTP (EUR). Secondary: brand perception (trust, safety perception) and price sensitivity.. Predictions: T1: Premium proposition will achieve at least 15% higher purchase intent and a WTP at least 10% above the low-cost proposition.; T2: Low-cost proposition will achieve at least 30% higher purchase intent and a WTP at least 20% below the premium proposition.. Decision rule: If premium purchase intent >= low-cost purchase intent + 15% AND premium WTP >= low-cost WTP + 10%, proceed with premium consumer proposition. If low-cost purchase intent >= premium purchase intent + 15% AND low-cost WTP >= premium WTP + 20%,. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes safety, reliability, and brand reputation from Lapp’s industrial leadership, targeting home automation and automotive aftermarket. Begin with a limited launch (e.g., a safety-focused charging kit for electric vehicles) and use the test results to decide on broader rollout. Target customer: Price-sensitive consumers in the home automation and automotive aftermarket who value safety and reliability, and are willing to pay a premium for Lapp’s industrial reputation.. Value proposition: A safety-focused, premium-priced consumer product leveraging Lapp’s industrial quality and brand trust, sold through direct-to-consumer channels to capture higher margins and build brand extension.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (500 German consumers, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness-to-pay for a premium safety proposition versus a low-cost volume proposition.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for Lapp components, the willingness of consumers to pay a premium for safety, and the competitive response from established consumer brands remain uncertain.. Would change if: If the test shows the low-cost proposition outperforms the premium proposition by at least 15% in purchase intent and 20% in willingness-to-pay, we would reconsider a low-cost volume strategy.; If new evidence shows Lapp already sells significant consumer volumes through existing channels, we would focus on expanding existing B2B segments rather than creating a new consumer proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the template-software offer and 72 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Subscription vs Entry-Level CNC Test" between T1; T2. Method: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups. Group A receives a €2,000 entry-level CNC router with a limited warranty and optional accessories. Group B receives the same router plus a 12-month subscription that includes software updates, cloud storage, and remote support. Both groups are offered a 10% discount if they sign up for the subscription within 12 weeks. The test runs for 12 weeks, and participants are contacted weekly to assess purchase intent, . Sample: 200 DIY woodworkers recruited via woodworking forums, social media, and local workshops. 100 participants per group.. Measure: Purchase conversion rate (percentage of participants who buy the router) and subscription uptake rate (percentage of participants who subscribe to the service).. Predictions: T1: Group A purchase rate ≥ 30%, Group B purchase rate ≤ 15% (entry-level machine meets DIY needs).; T2: Group B subscription rate ≥ 40%, Group A subscription rate ≤ 20% (subscription model provides convenience and ongoing updates).. Decision rule: If Group A purchase rate ≥ 30% and Group B purchase rate ≤ 15%, proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition around entry-level machines. If Group B subscription rate ≥ 40% and Group A subscription rate ≤ 20%, proceed with developing a subscription-based model for. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "DIY vs Contractor Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are recruited from a panel of DIY enthusiasts and professional contractors. They are shown a Sika-branded DIY sealant product description (easy-to-use, professional-grade results) and a Sika-branded contractor sealant product description (code-compliant, single supplier for both residential and commercial). They are then asked to indicate their likelihood to purchase each product on a 1‑10 scale. The. Sample: 200 participants: 100 DIY enthusiasts (recruited via DIY forums and social media) and 100 contractors (recruited via construction industry platforms).. Measure: Average purchase intent score for DIY product (T1) and contractor product (T2).. Predictions: T1: DIY participants will report a purchase intent score ≥ 7 for the DIY product and ≤ 5 for the contractor product.; T2: Contractors will report a purchase intent score ≥ 7 for the contractor product and ≤ 5 for the DIY product.. Decision rule: If the average DIY intent score ≥ 7 and contractor intent score ≤ 5, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting DIY (supports T1). If the average contractor intent score ≥ 7 and DIY intent score ≤ 5, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Professional-Grade vs Health-Focused Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions. Participants are recruited from a panel of home cooks and health-conscious consumers. They are randomly assigned to view one of two product descriptions: (A) Professional-grade vacuum sealer emphasizing professional-grade sealing, sous vide cooking, and bulk food processing; (B) Health-focused vacuum sealer emphasizing nutrient retention, waste reduction, and environmental benefits. After viewing the assigned description, participants are asked: 1) "How much would you be willing to pay for a vacuum sealer with this feature set?" (WTP open‑‑. Sample: 200 participants (100 home cooks, 100 health‑conscious consumers) recruited via an online panel; balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions.. Measure: Average willingness‑to‑pay (EUR) for each product description, and the difference in WTP between the two descriptions.. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP for professional‑grade messaging (average ≥ €250) compared to health‑focused messaging.; T2: Higher WTP for health‑focused messaging (average ≥ €250) compared to professional‑grade messaging.. Decision rule: If the difference in average WTP between the two messages exceeds €50 (e.g., professional‑grade WTP − health‑focused WTP ≥ €50), we conclude T1 is more likely. If the difference is less than €50, we conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is between €30‑. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for home cooks and culinary enthusiasts, emphasizing professional-grade sealing capabilities for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing, and price it at a premium (e.g., €200‑€300). Use existing B2B channels (dealers, online) to reach consumers and sell accessories (bags, seals) and service contracts to generate recurring revenue. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer motivations or willingness to pay for a vacuum sealer. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for home cooks and culinary enthusiasts, emphasizing professional-grade sealing capabilities for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing, and price it at a premium (e.g., €200‑€300). Use existing B2B channels (dealers, online) to reach consumers and sell accessories (bags, seals) and service contracts to generate recurring revenue. Target customer: Home cooks and serious amateur chefs who value professional-grade sealing for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing.. Value proposition: A consumer vacuum sealer that delivers professional-grade airtight sealing, reducing food waste and preserving freshness, while offering a compact, user‑friendly design and compatible accessories.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (200 participants, 10‑week survey) to measure willingness‑to‑pay for professional‑grade messaging versus health‑focused messaging.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for vacuum sealers, the willingness of home cooks to pay a premium, and the competitive landscape of existing consumer vacuum sealers remain uncertain.. Would change if: If the test shows health‑focused messaging yields higher willingness‑to‑pay (difference ≥ €50), we would shift to a health‑focused proposition.; If the test shows price sensitivity above €250, we would reconsider the premium pricing strategy.; If new evidence shows strong demand for health‑preserving vacuum sealing, we would incorporate nutrient retention messaging.. Test "Consumer Preference Test: Hobby vs Sustainability Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message versions: (A) Hobby-focused kit emphasizing creative spinning and craft appeal; (B) Sustainability-focused kit emphasizing recycled yarn and eco-friendly credentials. Both versions describe the same physical kit (spinning wheel, bobbin, accessories) with identical price point (e.g., €300). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 1‑10 scale and. Sample: 200 crafters recruited via craft forums and social media, balanced for gender and self‑reported spinning experience (beginner, intermediate, advanced).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) for each message version.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent for the hobby‑focused message (difference ≥ 1.5 points on the 10‑point scale).; T2: Higher purchase intent for the sustainability‑focused message (difference ≥ 1.5 points on the 10‑point scale).. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two messages is ≥ 1.5 points, proceed to develop the corresponding consumer proposition (either hobby‑focused kit or sustainability‑focused kit). If the difference is < 1.5 points, conclude that. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue focusing on the existing B2B offering and after-sales services for spinning mills. Any investment should be evaluated against a robust test of consumer willingness to pay and market size before committing. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Continue focusing on the existing B2B offering and after-sales services for spinning mills. Target customer: Rieter’s industrial spinning mill customers (3,000+), not individual consumers.. Value proposition: Maintain market leadership by providing high‑performance, reliable spinning systems and after‑sales support to mills, leveraging Rieter’s existing technology and service contracts.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Monitor consumer demand trends and conduct a small‑scale test (e.g., 200 crafters) to validate purchase intent before any major investment.. Uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay for a hobby‑focused spinning kit; the size of the market; whether sustainability messaging would drive purchase decisions.. Would change if: A controlled test shows purchase intent above 10% for a hobby‑focused kit priced at €300‑€500, or if a sustainability‑focused kit achieves a 15‑point lift in purchase intent compared to a hobby version.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Homebrewers and small‑batch food producers will purchase Krones equipment directly if they perceive it as a premium, sustainable, and time‑saving solution that reduces production costs and increases quality. Who benefits: Individual hobbyist brewers and small‑batch food producers who need reliable, efficient equipment for under‑10,000 L per batch.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers value reliability, ease of use, and environmental sustainability; they are willing to pay a premium for equipment that simplifies their production process and reduces waste.. How value is captured: Krones can capture value by pricing its consumer‑grade machines at a premium (e.g., €15,000‑€30,000 per unit) and offering subscription services for maintenance, capturing recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Homebrewers and small‑batch food producers are willing to invest in equipment that improves product quality and reduces labor.; Krones can design a consumer‑friendly product line that is easy to install and operate.; There is sufficient market awareness of Krones among this segment to drive direct purchases.. Predictions: If offered a direct‑to‑consumer product priced at €20,000 with a 2‑year warranty, at least 10% of surveyed homebrewers would express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Surveyed small‑batch food producers would report a willingness to pay a 20% premium for Krones equipment compared to competitors..

T2: Krones can capture value by offering a subscription‑based service for maintenance and consumables, enabling recurring revenue and a lower upfront purchase barrier for consumers. Who benefits: Homebrewers and small‑batch food producers who need reliable equipment but prefer lower initial cost and guaranteed support.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers value predictability and convenience; a subscription model removes the risk of equipment failure and simplifies cash flow, making them more willing to adopt Krones equipment.. How value is captured: Krones captures value through monthly or annual subscription fees (e.g., €150‑€250 per unit) and bundled consumables, generating recurring revenue and a higher lifetime value per customer.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a subscription fee for maintenance and consumables that covers normal wear and tear.; Krones can scale a subscription platform and delivery of consumables without significant additional overhead.; There is sufficient market awareness of Krones among this segment to drive subscription sign‑ups.. Predictions: If offered a subscription model with a 2‑year maintenance contract and consumables, at least 15% of surveyed homebrewers would subscribe within 12 weeks.; Small‑batch food producers would report a willingness to pay a 10% premium for a subscription‑based service compared to a one‑time purchase..

Test "Subscription vs Premium Direct Purchase Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice experiment with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 2,000 U.S. homebrewers and small‑batch food producers recruited via hobbyist forums, social media, and industry newsletters.. Measure: Proportion choosing the subscription model (WTP €150‑€250 per year) vs the premium direct‑purchase model (WTP €20,000‑€30,000). Secondary measure: stated maximum price for Krones equipment.. Predictions: T1: At least 35% will choose the premium direct purchase model, with a WTP of €25,000 or higher, indicating willingness to pay a premium for Krones equipment.; T2: At least 35% will choose the subscription model, with a WTP of €150‑€250 per year, indicating willingness to pay for a lower upfront cost and maintenance service.. Decision rule: If the proportion choosing the premium direct purchase model ≥ 35% and average WTP ≥ €25,000, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium direct buyers. If the proportion choosing the subscription model ≥ 35% and average WTP ≥ €150‑€250, proceed with a subscription‑based service. If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium, direct‑purchase homebrewers and small‑batch food producers who value reliability, efficiency, and sustainability. Price the equipment at a premium (e.g., €20,000‑€30,000 per unit) and offer subscription maintenance for a lower upfront cost. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium, direct‑purchase homebrewers and small‑batch food producers who value reliability, efficiency, and sustainability. Price the equipment at a premium (e.g., €20,000‑€30,000 per unit) and offer subscription maintenance for a lower upfront cost. Target customer: Homebrewers and small‑batch food producers (under 10,000 L per batch) in the United States who seek reliable, efficient equipment and are willing to pay a premium for quality.. Value proposition: High‑performance, easy‑to‑install brewhouse equipment that reduces production time and waste, backed by Krones’s proven industrial reliability and a subscription maintenance option to lower upfront cost.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed subscription vs premium direct‑purchase test (2,000 U.S. hobbyists/producers) to measure willingness to pay and choice between models. Test "Consumer Preference Survey for Automatic Doors" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized presentation of two product concepts: (1) an integrated automatic door system marketed as part of a smart home ecosystem, and (2) a subscription‑based accessibility service featuring the same automatic door. Participants are asked about willingness to pay, purchase intent, and perceived value for each concept.. Sample: 500 homeowners and caregivers in Japan and the United States who have accessibility needs and are considering home renovations. Recruitment via panel providers to ensure demographic diversity.. Measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who indicate purchase intent for the smart home ecosystem concept (T1) versus the subscription service concept (T2). Secondary measures: maximum willingness to pay (WTP) for each concept, and perceived importance of remote support and software updates.. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent for the smart home ecosystem concept will be at least 30% higher than for the subscription service concept.; T2: Purchase intent for the subscription service concept will be at least 15% higher than for the smart home ecosystem concept.. Decision rule: If the smart home ecosystem purchase intent exceeds the subscription service intent by at least 15 percentage points (i.e., smart home ≥ 45%, subscription ≤ 30%), T1 is favoured. If subscription service intent exceeds smart home intent by at least 15 percentage points (i.e., subscription ≥ 45%, smart home ≤ 30%), T2 is favoured. If the difference is less than 15 points, results are inconclusive and further. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.
